The tree walk now runs on plain Vita arithmetic, and each leaf of the tree gets a compact block built from the model's own triangles the first time it is visited (a bounding sphere and the plane of each triangle, four at a time for the Vita's vector unit), so a leaf is one quick pass; only triangles the ray can actually cross go on to the game's own exact hit test, so the hits are the game's. With it, the old shortcut that reused a ray's answer for up to 5 frames (so a character could step into the camera's view up to 5 frames late) is off: every ray is answered every frame.
rows.result: Vita3K 222 MHz: each ray test ~130 us instead of ~190-260, the tree walks ~4x faster; the main thread 0.4-1.7 ms a frame faster riding in the attract demo, even (within +-0.5 ms) at the shrine, the altar and on route 6, where the old 5-frame reuse saved about as much as the new walk. Checks: the new and the old answers compared on about 1.5 million tests (attract, route 6, the console card's shrine save): no difference since the second build, hit points within 0.4 mm. No crash. On by default; console A/B pending.

rows.summary: Fourth step on the helper thread that does far-away characters' body work on another Vita core. Last round it seemed to wake ten times slower after round 110's display timing; measuring showed that was the Mac running the emulator being overloaded by other builds at the time, not the game (with the display timing on and off at once the delay was the same and rose with the Mac's load). Keeping characters that seemed to gain nothing on the main thread turned out to cost more (about 1-1.4 ms a frame), so that stays off. Instead the helper now checks its own account every few seconds and pauses in scenes where handing characters over costs the main thread more than it saves (riding in the attract demo), then tries again. The helper path is now on by default.
rows.result: Vita3K 222 MHz, quiet runs: shrine +0.6 to +0.7 ms a frame, the plain (route 6) +0.2 to +0.5, attract riding from -1.1 to 0.0 / +0.45. Check mode: 0 differences in every comparison; the old 144-byte mismatch in the hand-over's self-check is gone. No crash, including loading the console's save. The console's own A/B log decides whether it stays on.

rows.summary: Round 113's plan item 6 (the game's own script, AI and camera code still running as translated PS2 code, and the machinery that switches between the scripts) measured piece by piece. It turned out flat: hundreds of small functions, the camera alone about a hundred of them, none worth more than a few hundredths of a millisecond, and most of the rest belongs to the particle, collision and character work other rounds are doing. Two whole pieces were there and are now plain Vita code with the same results: the system that links streamed-in game modules together by name (while riding it re-checked ~2 200 names and ~600 module links every dozen frames, 5-9 ms each time on the emulator), and the game's memory allocator. The script switching itself would only get cheaper by no longer keeping the PS2's saved registers in memory, which would make the port inexact for ~0.3 ms; not done.
rows.result: Vita3K 222 MHz: the module-linking pass 3.6x faster per call (1.7 ms instead of 6.0, every dozen frames while riding; its slowest calls were 6-20 ms frame spikes), the allocator about 4x less time; together ~1.5% of the main thread riding by the sampler (~0.9 ms of the console's 60 ms), less elsewhere. Too small for the emulator's in-run comparison to resolve (its noise is 1-3 ms). Exact: 0 differences in every check (thousands of compared calls); no crash in the attract demo, route 6 or the console save's load. Far below the plan's -5 ms: that time is spread too thinly to rewrite piece by piece.

rows.summary: Second and third steps of rebuilding collision for the Vita. Measured first where collision's time goes after round 115: it is spread thin (about 15% of the main thread, nothing above 3%), mostly the per-object bookkeeping of the ray tests and the character's repeated passes over the list of nearby surfaces (landing, foot placement, sliding). Built: the nearby-surface list keeps, for the frame, where each surface's plane lives, so the repeated passes test it straight away instead of looking it up through the object each time; the slide's pass skips the calls the game would answer 'no' to at once; the terrain search no longer queues the branches the ray cannot reach; the ray tests' matrix math skips safety clamps that cannot change the result; empty bookkeeping lists are no longer handed to a function that does nothing with them. Also found the cause of round 115's few unexplained differences right after loading a save: the AI's path rays with an endpoint at 'infinity', which now go to the game's own code.
rows.result: Vita3K 222 MHz: every touched function is faster in the same run (terrain search ~2-5%, ray tests ~2-3%, surface-list passes ~2-8%, list flushes ~4-9%), about 0.1-0.15 ms a frame in total; the whole-frame A/B is at its noise floor (the largest riding run +0.14 ms, route 6 -0.21). Checks: every answer compared with the game's own over about 3 million ray tests and 10 million surface-list decisions (attract riding, route 6, the altar, the console card's shrine save): 0 differences in this round's parts; round 115's after-load differences gone; two rare cases left from round 115's ray walk (one surface tie at a triangle edge per ~500 000 rays, one camera ray at an edge in the shrine run). No crash. Off by default (no clear whole-frame win everywhere: riding +0.14, route 6 -0.21, within noise); the console's A/B, which turns them on, decides. The after-load fix is on.

rows.summary: Global speedups that cover all the code at once instead of one function at a time. The compiler now optimises the hand-written Vita code and the runtime with a profile of how the game really runs (profile-guided optimisation, trained in the emulator on the attract demo, the shrine, the ride to the sixth colossus and a save load): the main thread is about 1-3 ms (3-6%) faster in every scene measured, with no change in what the code computes (all in-game self-checks: 0 differences). The order of the code in memory was rebuilt from fresh profiles so the hot code sits together again (the old order predated most of the native code). Applying the profile to the recompiled game too gave nothing measurable in the emulator, so it is off by default and shipped as a second console build to compare. The character worker jobs are off by default on the Vita after the console test showed them losing time.

First round under the new rule (a port, not an emulator: the same gameplay and picture, not the same bits). The particles' per-particle step now runs as ordinary C++ floats straight from the emitter loop (no PS2 call frame, no PS2 float emulation), and a particle damage test that did nothing was called for every particle every frame and is now skipped. The emitter parameter copy goes through host pointers. Collision: the console's round 119 log showed the new ray walk was faster on the Vita but lost because the old memo (reuse a ray's answer while it barely moves) had been switched off with it; a new memo reuses an answer only while the ray stays within 1 cm and nothing it could hit has moved (each object near the ray is fingerprinted once a frame, objects far from it are ignored).
rows.result: Vita3K 222 MHz: particle step 2.2-2.4 vs 6.6-6.9 us a particle (~90 a frame riding); ray tests on route 6's plain 142 vs 185 us (55% answered from the memo), riding even (161 vs 157), shrine even. Whole-frame A/B +0.4..+1.55 ms of the game thread for the round in five runs (noise +-1 ms). Checks: 1.04 M particles compared field by field (2 fields over 1e-4 relative); 54 000 kept ray answers all agree on hit / no hit with a fresh test, 2-3% name the neighbouring triangle across an edge, hit points within 1.3 cm. Far below the -5 ms target: the rest of collision (object loop, finders, ground fill) is next.

rows.summary: Collision as a native object system, second part. The surfaces a character keeps around it (the lists the ground fill builds every frame) now live in a host cache with their whole triangles, and the probes against them (landing, foot placement, slide) run as one pass over host data with the original's own arithmetic, instead of a chain of guest-memory lookups and a call per surface; the cache is kept valid per object (an object that moves has only its own surfaces checked again). The ray tests' object / part loop keeps its state in host variables instead of the PS2's stack frame, with plain math for the 'is this part near the ray' tests.
rows.result: Vita3K 222 MHz, same build and frames, round off vs on: collision 12.5% -> 9.9% of the main thread riding (ray tests and their object loop 3.0 -> 2.0, the surface probes 3.6 -> 2.5); per call in the same run the surface probes 19% and the ray tests 12% faster; the whole-frame A/B +0.24..+0.44 ms (noise about as large). Checks against the original in the same state: 360 000 surface probes and 265 000 ray tests, all the same answer, surface and point. Replays of route 6 with the round on and off: Wander and Agro at the same positions to 0.0001 units through the shrine. Far below the -4 ms target: the object loop is now the largest collision item and is memory-bound; the ground fill's skinned step and the tree walk are next.

rows.summary: Characters and camera: the guest code they share for 'a point / rotation on something' (the geometry pointer getters, the quaternion-to-matrix and half-turn helpers, a character node's frame) and four character control helpers (Wander's 90-frame movement history, a rotation's turn about the vertical, a motion root track's key, the option nodes' getters, the last two now made in place by the native node passes) were rewritten as plain C++ / NEON. The camera itself turned out to be a thousand small functions with no hot spot, so a tool was written that turns whole guest subtrees into C++ automatically (1 732 camera and character functions): it ran correctly but was slower than the existing recompiled code in the profiler, so it is kept as a tool and left out of the build, with what it would need. A cache for the camera's collision-ray filter was also slower and was dropped.
rows.result: Vita3K 222 MHz, the profiler with the same build and window: the rewritten getters went from 1.0-1.1% of the game thread to under 0.3% (-0.64% in the attract demo, -0.97% at the shrine): about 0.3-0.5 ms a frame on the console. Whole-frame A/B within its +-1 ms noise (attract +0.05..+0.36, shrine -1.17). Checks: every rewritten function compared call by call with the original on the same state (float words within 0.2%): no differences beyond float rounding. The automatic C++ conversion of 1 732 functions was 12-50% slower than the recompiled code it replaced and the collision-filter cache 50% slower, so neither ships. Far below the -3 ms target: the camera has no hot spot left to rewrite by hand.

rows.summary: Is there garbage in the code that slows the game? 130 rounds of logs, timers, checks and A/B switches were counted call by call (a special counting build) and priced with the console's own unit costs. The frame log's per-thread CPU readout (14 kernel calls a frame, 0.8 ms on the game thread on the console) moved to the log thread, which now also formats every line; a much cheaper console log setup (frame summary only); and a release build for playing with every check, per-call timer, A/B rotation and profiler hook compiled out.
rows.result: With the old console log flags the diagnostics cost about 1.0-1.2 ms of the game thread, 1.3-1.8 ms of the render thread (per-draw timers) and ~1.5 ms of the other cores on the console (estimates from counted calls x measured console costs); the new setup removes nearly all of it. With no log flags at all the old build already paid almost nothing. Vita3K: clock reads 1 743 -> 274 a frame; the release build's game thread -3..-8% in the profiler (noise ~1 ms).

rows.summary: A tool that turns the game's remaining recompiled functions into native C++ by machine (tools/lift_d1.py), built so that the decomp can scale toward 100%. Round 126's attempt rewrote every instruction itself and ran 6-10x slower; this one keeps the recompiler's own, proven instruction code and only moves the CPU state into fast local variables, writing it back to the emulated CPU only where something can look at it (calls, returns, the scheduler). It lifts 98% of the 8 163 functions still recompiled. Proven on two areas: all of Math (102 functions) and the boot program's 519 small leaf helpers (matrix, vector, table, pad and timer helpers), 621 functions in all, behind one switch (SOTC_LIFTD1, on).
rows.result: Decomp: 1 492 of 9 024 functions native (16.5%, was 9.5%), 16.9% of the code (was 14.8%), Math 100%. Exact: every checked call of the 281 lifted functions the test runs reached was compared with the original on the same state (attract demo, the console card's walk and ride: 235 000 checks): no register ever different, the only differences single memory bytes other threads wrote meanwhile. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, same build, switch on / off): the lifted set 1.20% -> 1.03% of the game thread (15% faster); statically 95% of the original's instructions on the hot path. Pictures in the attract demo, walking and riding unchanged.

rows.summary: The next batch of machine-converted functions, picked by how much of the game thread they take: the top 1 300 of the still-recompiled code were converted and run through every check (call-by-call comparison with the original on the Mac, A/B timing and the console card's walk and ride on Vita3K). The checks found three real bugs in the converter and fixed them (a delay-slot case, values written back on paths that never changed them, and 64-bit values passed in registers the converter took for 32-bit ones, which kept the walk on the loading screen). Only the 245 leaf functions (no calls) ship this round, behind SOTC_LIFTD2 (on); the call-heavy rest waits for D3 to re-check with the fixes.
rows.result: Decomp: 1 737 of 9 024 functions native (19.3%, was 16.5%), 18.4% of the code, 83.8% of calls. Exact: the shipped functions compared with the original on the same state in the attract demo, walk and ride, 0 register differences (the only differences single memory bytes other threads wrote meanwhile). Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, in-run A/B): the leaves 12-28% faster than the recompiled code, about 0.2-0.4% of the game thread; the whole frame within the A/B's noise. Pictures: walk (29 000 frames), ride and the attract demo normal, Wander and Agro on the ground.

rows.summary: D1's machine-converted functions regenerated with the converter's three D2 fixes (235 of 621 changed), and D2's call-heavy functions converted and checked: 534 candidates, 414 ship behind SOTC_LIFTD3 (on). Each was compared call by call with the original on the Mac (attract demo, the console card's walk and ride), and the walk, ride and attract demo were run on Vita3K with the converted code on from boot and under the A/B. Left out: 37 that no test run reached and 83 that the A/B measured slower. No wild return or fault appeared, so the stack-pointer guard D2 proposed was not needed. The regenerated D1 also ran alone and under the rotating A/B with no slowdown.
rows.result: Decomp: 2 151 of 9 024 functions native (23.8%, was 19.3%), 23.3% of the code, 88.2% of calls, 75.1% of the game thread's time in native code (D2: 71.1%). Exact: the final 414 compared on 276 569 calls in three Mac runs, with 412 reached. There were 0 register differences in the converted code itself: the one register difference was a hardware timer value a callee leaves in a0. The remaining memory differences are the timer word and bytes that other threads write, as in a control run. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, in-run A/B): the set 2.7% faster than the recompiled code (4.57% vs 4.70% of the game thread); whole frame off minus on +0.55 +- 0.54 ms. Pictures: walk, ride, attract and the console env's rotation normal, Wander and Agro on the ground.

rows.summary: The converter learned what every function and everything it calls reads and writes (a whole-program summary), so a converted function could keep values in its own variables across calls instead of storing and reloading them. It is exact (compared call by call with the original on the Mac), but on the Vita's CPU it was 5-6% slower overall in an in-run A/B, so it is used only in the 8 functions it made faster. Then the next batch: 607 functions converted (D2 and D3's slower ones retried, the 36 indirect-call ones, the next of the ranking); 429 ship behind SOTC_LIFTD4 (on) after the A/B cut 82 slower, 5 differed from the original and 91 no test run reached. A test-harness bug that stopped checks after thread switches was found and fixed.
rows.result: Decomp: 2 580 of 9 024 functions native (28.6%, was 23.8%), 27.8% of the code, 90.5% of calls, 78.0% of the game thread's time in native code (D3: 75.1%). Exact: every shipped function compared with the original (224 355 checks in six Mac runs plus an exploration run), 0 register differences; memory differences are the timer words and bytes other threads write, as in a control run. The 36 indirect-call functions D2 linked to wild returns ran on Vita3K (25 ship) with none. Pictures: walk, ride, attract and the console env's rotation normal, Wander and Agro on the ground.

rows.summary: The converter can now paste small functions straight into the converted code that calls them (no call, values stay in registers), behind a check that the function table still holds that function. It is exact, but on the Vita's CPU it was close to break-even overall in an in-run A/B (1.4% faster for the functions involved), so it is used only in the 15 callers measured faster in two runs. The natives' fallbacks to the original code (about 3% of the game thread ran there) now get converted copies too: 44 ship. And the next batch: 86 functions behind SOTC_LIFTD5 (on), 55 new from a fresh profile and 31 of D4's slower ones that are no longer slower.
rows.result: Decomp: 2 666 of 9 024 functions native (29.5%, was 28.6%), 28.9% of the code, 91.7% of calls. Exact: all 145 shipped functions compared with the original in the attract demo, walk and ride (159 649 checks), 0 register differences. Speed: the shipped sets are faster than what they replace in the A/B (the batch -22%, the fallbacks -7%, the inlined callers -27%), but the whole frame stays within the A/B's noise: function-level conversion has no large speed left in it; 30 fps needs subsystem rewrites. Pictures: walk, ride, attract and the console env's rotation normal, Wander and Agro on the ground.

rows.summary: The six functions D5 left out with 'register mismatches' were not converter bugs: the test harness compared five of them with the hand-written native code that holds their table slot instead of the original code (fixed; with it they match). Then a new test for code that waits or switches threads, which could not be tested before because it was run twice: the original code now runs once for real while every call, wait and hardware access it makes is recorded, and the converted code is replayed against that record, compared at every one of those points and at the end. With it D5's three waits that hung the Mac's load are checked, and 439 functions that may block were converted and checked; 285 ship behind SOTC_LIFTD6 (on), the rest were cut for speed. D5's 44 shipped fallback copies, which had been checked against the natives, were re-checked against the original: all exact.
rows.result: Decomp: 2 951 of 9 024 functions native (32.7%, was 29.5%), 34.4% of the code, 92.5% of calls, 80.4% of the game thread's time in native code (D5: 79.6%). Exact: every shipped function (the 285, the fallback copy and D5's 44 fallback copies) compared with the original at every call, wait and hardware access and at the end, in five Mac runs (walk, ride, attract): 0 register, clock or event differences; memory differences are single bytes other threads wrote, as in a control run. Speed: neutral on the Vita (the shipped set 0.1% slower to 8.5% faster in two A/Bs; 154 functions that were slower cut). Pictures: walk, ride, attract and the console env's rotation normal, Wander and Agro on the ground.

rows.summary: Decomp D7. A new speed measure: the A/B now switches the lifted code on or off at random every frame, so both sides see the same scenes; two runs agree (per-function correlation 0.93, where D6's window A/B disagreed in sign). The trace check now covers the inlined and summarized calls too. Re-checking D3-D5 with it found a real converter bug: the original's sign branches test only the low 32 bits, and the converted code tested 64. It is fixed in 199 already shipped functions. Two more bugs turned up in the new batch (a jump-table form, a 128-bit write-back). D7's batch is everything the Mac's walk, ride, attract and exploration runs reach, plus the earlier rounds' speed cuts: 1 681 functions ship behind SOTC_LIFTD7 (on).
rows.result: Decomp: 4 625 of 9 024 functions native (51.3%, was 32.7%), 52.1% of the code, 96.8% of calls; 83.7% of the game thread in native code (was 80.4%). Exact: every shipped function checked with the trace check on its current code, 0 register / clock / event differences; D3-D5 re-checked: 862 of 879, 0 after the fix. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B): the shipped set took about 80% of its recompiled time, about 0.6% of the game thread (chosen with the same runs, so the figure is optimistic); 89 functions slower in both runs, or not measurable, left out. Pictures: walk, ride, attract demo and the rotation walk normal, Wander and Agro on the ground.

rows.summary: Decomp D8: the particles and effects area, and new ways into the game. New routes: a new game (the opening cutscene, then the altar) and a teleport test aid (SOTC_TELEPORT, through the game's own warp) that puts Wander at any colossus' arena from the console card. On Avion's lake that reached the boss's set-up and release, arrows into the water and swimming. Two findings on the count itself. The worker thread's wrappers had made about 130 particle-module functions look decompiled when their original code still ran, and decomp_status now counts without them. And D8's first test passes had silently run the old two-run check instead of the trace check (a shell quoting slip): they were thrown away and redone. 365 functions ship behind SOTC_LIFTD8 (on), and docs/particles_map.md maps the particle code for the redesign round S1.
rows.result: Particles and effects: 91 of 116 functions decompiled on the honest count (about 58 before D8; 98 of 116 on the old count, which included the wrappers). The other 25 need a colossus fight, a dive or a ledge, or are never called at all; docs say what would reach each one. Whole game: 4 856 of 9 024 functions (53.8%), 55.6% of the code, 96.4% of calls on the honest count (old count 4 916, 54.5%). Exact: every shipped function checked by the trace check on its final code, 0 register / clock / event differences. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B): no function slower in both runs; the set +0.01% / -0.02% of the game thread (noise). Pictures: walk, ride, attract, Avion's lake and the rotation walk normal, Wander and Agro on the ground.

rows.summary: Round S1, the first subsystem redesign, with particles as the pilot. A semantic decomp: ptcl_types.h names the guest data (the particle record, the node and emitter, the effect set, the LOD record, the 48-byte draw record, the manager's globals), with who else reads each. The PS2 shape went from the hot paths. The three sprite drawers now build their records in plain host floats (four lanes at a time, NEON on the Vita) straight into the renderer's job: no guest display list, no copy back out, no guest call per particle. Each emitter's particles are stepped as one batch on values worked out once per emitter, bit for bit the same as before. Behind SOTC_S1PTCL (on; A/B s1ptcl). The original stays one switch away. Round 91's worker job stays off: on the console it cost the game thread 2.5-3 ms, because cores 1-2 are already busy. Particle work can leave core 0 only once it is host code with no guest context.
rows.result: Equivalence, checked in-run from the same state. Per draw against the original's job: 104 000 draws / 28 M words in the attract demo and 648 000 draws / 13 M words on Avion's lake route. Count, texture, layer, blend and environment 0 differ. Under 0.0001% of words exceed 1e-5 / 1e-4, all of them the cos lane of the sin / cos pair near +-1 (an angle error under 0.012 deg). Whole RAM after the original against after S1: 1 050 checks, 0 words differ outside the dead stack and the display list's room. The particle step: 3.2-3.4 M steps, 0 differ (bit-exact). Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved per-frame A/B, sampler): S1's code costs 34-54% less than the code it replaces, saving 0.42% of the game thread in the attract demo and 0.84% on the lake route (about 0.1-0.37 ms a frame). Frame times: no difference measurable (six runs each within 2 SE, -0.13..0 +- 0.1-0.2 ms). The console A/B decides (env-console: s1ptcl rotating every 600 frames). A first batch read its values through a reference across may_alias stores and ran 1.7x slower; it was caught by the A/B and fixed. Pictures (Vita3K, on / off): Agro's gallop dust, the shrine's mist and light, the lake's splashes all as the original. No exact 0, Wander and Agro on the ground. Not reached: the boss's blood and the weak point's glow (they need a hit on a colossus).

rows.summary: Decomp D9: collision and physics, the next subsystem after the particles. New routes on Avion's lake and in Valus' canyon (falls and drops, swims into the pillars, climbing tries on the canyon wall, a new game to Valus), and a test aid that prints which function a run reached first and when. One lake run got Wander onto a pillar by an edge hang and reached the hanging and climbing code, but no later run repeated it. A second honesty count: natives that fall back to the original code. 38 hand-written natives still ran their original code on the routes, some millions of times a run (GetLayoutClass); 9 of them are collision natives. D9 gives 27 of them checked converted copies and makes converted functions serve the natives' fallbacks too. A converter bug fixed (long jump tables lost their later cases). 136 functions ship behind SOTC_LIFTD9 (on), and docs/collision_map.md maps collision for the redesign round S2.
rows.result: Collision and physics: 169 of 319 functions decompiled (158 after D8), 166 of them in every path (149 after D8 on that count); the other 150 need recorded gameplay (hanging, climbing, fights, trigger volumes) or are debug / never called, and docs say what would reach each one. Whole game (honest count): 4 965 of 9 024 functions (55.0%), 57.1% of the code, 96.4% of calls. Exact: every shipped function checked by the trace check on its final code, 0 register / clock / event differences; RAM bytes in 12 functions shown to be the harness's own (a control run shows them too). Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B): 5 converted copies slower in both runs were cut; the set -0.12% / -0.17% of the game thread. Collision is 13.7-21.6% of the Vita3K game thread, almost all host code already.

rows.summary: Round S2, collision part 1. A semantic decomp: coll_types.h names the collision data (surface ids, the collision DB, part and surface records, the split tree, the hit record, the game's per-frame caches, the finder lists). The profile first: on Avion's lake the two water probes were the largest collision items (4.1% of the game thread), and each character's contact list was clipped 15-23 times a frame entry by entry through fin125's hash cache. Two host-side changes. Finder lists get host views (the id words, the cache slots, the planes as structure of arrays), used while nothing they rest on has moved, with the plane test four entries at a time in the same NEON operations (the same bits) and a sphere pre-test; the keep pass reads them too. The water probes run their per-triangle body only for the triangles that can decide the answer (an xz box with a margin, the height between the ends, the last triangle always), instead of three outer products and two divisions for every triangle. Behind SOTC_S2COLL (on; A/B s2coll; knobs SOTC_S2COLL_VIEWS / _WATER). Moving queries to another core was assessed and left out: every query's caller uses its answer at once, and cores 1-2 are busy.
rows.result: Equivalence, checked in-run from the same state with no tolerance: every view clip against the guest's own ClipCollisionDB loop, every keep test against fin125, every water probe both ways with its work blocks: 0 differences in 1.46 M view clips, 5.7 M keep tests and 0.49 M water probes on the lake route and the attract demo. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved per-frame A/B, two seeds): on the lake route the game thread does about 2.2 ms a frame less (finder clips -0.43..-0.45 ms, z 18-20; water probes -1.7 ms, z 32-56; the views' code 60% of what it replaces by the sampler, z 65-76), collision about 22% -> 17% of the game thread; in the attract demo 0.2-0.3%. Frame times do not resolve it (all within about 2 SE), as in S1. The first water form was slower (std::fmax / fmin are library calls on the Vita's VFPv3) and was fixed before shipping. Pictures: swimming, the gallop and the walk as the original; No exact 0. The console A/B decides (env-console: s2coll, liftd9, s1ptcl rotating every 600 frames).

rows.summary: Decomp D10: characters and motion, the subsystem after collision. A new game now reaches the first colossus in about 2 600 frames (one START press skips the opening), and teleports by place, an object list and a function probe put Wander on Valus' plateau: Valus walks to him and stamps, Wander dies and retries, and the fight's code runs (attack IK, the quake hit test, the parts' damage getters, the game over flow). 98 functions ship behind SOTC_LIFTD10 (on): 97 converted ones and the first hand-written replacement of a function the converter made slower (Agro's cloth callback, now faster than the original in both speed runs). docs/characters_map.md maps the characters' code for the redesign round S3, with what each character's frame shares with the others.
rows.result: Characters and motion: 646 of 1 206 functions decompiled (623 after D9), 66.0% of the code. Whole game (honest count): 5 063 of 9 024 functions (56.1%), 58.3% of the code, 96.5% of calls. Exact: 108 functions checked by the trace check (and the hand native by the two-leg check, 700 checks), 0 differences. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B): ten hot functions the converter makes slower were cut again; the shipped set is neutral (+0.003% / +0.007% of the game thread). The rest of the area needs recorded play (climbing a colossus, hitting weak points, the other fifteen colossi) or hand-written replacements for the ten hot ones.

rows.summary: Round S3, characters and motion. First the race D10 found: the motion-key decoder shared one static buffer between the game thread and the guest worker (off the Vita); now one per thread. A semantic decomp: chara_types.h names the skeleton, motion resources, motion and IK records, gazes and about 90 fields of the character class. The profile first: the area is ~16% of the game thread and flat; only the skeleton's pose passes 1%. The pose now runs over a host copy of each skeleton's shape (the bones in visit order with their parents; links and offsets checked against the game's on every call), one flat loop with the same arithmetic as before and no per-call walk of the links. An A9 finding: the Vita's GCC turns NEON float compares into scalar compares with pipeline syncs; the pose's normalisation now uses an integer compare with the same result. Kept bones (reuse of unchanged bones) and a second core (half a skeleton or half a motion's channels on a worker thread, with work stealing) were built, checked exact and measured: both left off (too few bones kept; jobs of 10-20 us gain ~0.05 ms while the worker spins on a tenth of a core). And why S1 / S2's frame-time A/Bs read zero: the analysis paired each frame with the next frame's switch state; aligned, S2's lake saving shows as +2.1-2.2 ms a frame.
rows.result: Exact: every pose compared bit for bit with round 82's in-run (586 000 poses, 15.5 M bones on the attract demo, the lake and the ride), every split decode with a whole one: 0 differences, no tolerance. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B, two seeds): the pose code 74-83% of round 82's by the sampler (z 29-52), frame times +0.13 / +0.18 ms (attract) and +0.18 / +0.36 ms (lake), z 2.3-4.9; SOTC_S3CHARA on. Shipped S3 adds no thread. Frame-time A/Bs now resolve 0.1-0.2 ms with the alignment fixed.

rows.summary: Decomp D11: the display and models area, and an A9 fix S3 found. The Vita's GCC turns NEON's vector float compares into four scalar compares with pipeline syncs; a small header now gives the same masks from integer compares (checked over every input pattern: no difference in about 118 billion cases). Tried at eight places, kept at the five the sampler shows faster in both seeds (the 2D quad emitter, the cloth meshes, the walk's sphere and plane select, the leaf texture coordinates, the collision leaf); the other three went back. Two native renderer fixes: the model LOD is read signed as the game does, and the host's layer stack follows the game's own pushes and pops. The frame-time columns of D7-S2's interleaved A/Bs are marked invalid (the off-by-one S3 found). 278 functions converted, 108 checked exact on the walk, the pause menu, the attract demo and the lake; ten display ones were slower and cut: 98 ship behind SOTC_LIFTD11 (on), 19 of them display (the gl* immediate calls, the menu's sprite functions). docs/display_map.md maps the area for the draw-path redesign (S4).
rows.result: Display and models: 507 of 977 functions decompiled (489 after D10), 61.6% of the code. Whole game (honest count): 5 161 of 9 024 functions (57.2%), 59.4% of the code, 97.2% of calls. Exact: 108 functions checked by the trace check, 0 differences; the integer compares exhaustively checked. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B, two seeds): the kept compare sites save 0.06-0.08 ms a frame by the sampler (frame A/B +0.11 ms on average, +0.26 ms on the lake with seed 7); the shipped converted functions take 62-81% of the generated code's time. Game thread on the Vita: 83.5% native, 4.0% recompiled MIPS.

rows.summary: Round S4, display and draw prep. With the native renderer drawing (always on the Vita) the game still built PS2 graphics packets that nothing read and the host read some of them back. A semantic decomp first: disp_types.h names the display's records (models, surfaces, draw packets, instances, the palette layout, the display list). The profile: draw prep is a fifth of the game thread, flat; the PS2-packet side about 3-4.5%. Ten screen passes (the water reflection set-up, depth fog and background, the shadow reset and reduce, the depth of field, the refraction copy, the bloom chain ...) now run as host-only variants that keep only what the game and the renderer read (the ripple clock, the shadow handshake, the bloom's eased values, the fog and bloom notes), building no packets. The packet-level hooks no longer re-read their debugging switches on every call (an A9 finding: each such static costs a memory barrier per call). The skinned palettes are no longer read back a second time at the display list's kick when the game has not rewritten them: the worker keeps the hook's read. Moving draw prep to another core was measured and left: S4 removes work rather than moving it.
rows.result: Checked in-run: every replaced pass's original run with a RAM snapshot, every written word classified, 1 297 calls on the attract demo, the lake and the ride: 0 unknown writes, 0 differences in the kept values, the renderer's state or its draw emissions; 147 000 kick palettes compared with the worker's copy, 0 differ. Pictures unchanged. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B, two seeds): frame time -0.50 / -0.69 ms on the attract demo and -1.17 / -0.89 ms at the lake (z 3.7-10.8); the game thread 0.75-1.17 ms a frame less busy; the render thread and the hook worker unchanged (the render thread +0.3-0.4 ms at the lake, z under 3). SOTC_S4DISP on.

rows.summary: A sweep for what the Vita's compiler turns into slow Cortex-A9 code in hot paths, found with the emulator's sampler and fixed without changing behaviour. Settings read once into function-level statics cost a memory barrier on every call: 90 such values are now read once at start. Equality checks of fixed-size blocks (memcmp, 1% of the game thread) are now word compares at 82 places. The scheduler's divisions (the A9 has no divide instruction) are now multiplies, two of its lookups are cached, and a per-call thread-local store nobody read is skipped. Every part can be A/B tested on its own.
rows.result: Exact: the divisions checked over 1.1e11 inputs and the compares over 1.6e7, 0 differ; every hoisted value equal to the original; the S2 / S3 / S4 checks 0 differences; pictures unchanged. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B, two seeds): frame time -0.30 / -0.44 ms on the attract demo and -0.71 / -0.75 ms at the lake (z 5.5-11.4); the game thread 0.31-0.73 ms a frame less busy. Per part at the lake: the compares -0.25 / -0.37 ms, the scheduler -0.28 / -0.41 ms; the hoisted settings not measurable in Vita3K (a barrier costs one instruction there), kept for the console. SOTC_A9SWEEP on.

rows.summary: Decomp D12: more of the game converted, chosen from what the test routes actually run. Most still-unconverted code belongs to colossi the console save never meets (only one colossus is in the world at a time). A new test aid calls the game's own switch of the current colossus, so two new routes visit colossi 5 to 16 from the console save: the functions the routes reach and that were still unconverted nearly doubled (291 to 566), mostly script, characters and collision. The converter learned three more code patterns (one of them the most-called function left, a message send with 29 million calls a run). 455 functions converted, 282 checked exact on the colossus routes and the pause menu; six were slower and cut: 276 ship behind SOTC_LIFTD12 (on), 35 of them script and 10 collision.
rows.result: Whole game (honest count): 5 437 of 9 024 functions (60.2%, 57.2% after D11), 63.4% of the code, 97.6% of calls. Script and events 267 of 633 (232), collision 184 of 317 (174), characters 704 of 1 206 (651). Exact: 282 functions checked by the trace check, 0 differences. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B, two seeds): frame time neutral in all four runs (within 0.1 ms); the message send about 30% cheaper converted. Boots and runs with the console's free memory (Vita3K, 89 MB taken).

rows.summary: Round S5, the second particle round after S1. Each frame the game stepped every live particle (moving it, bouncing it off the floor or ceiling, ageing it) on the game thread, and the draws then computed each particle's rotation and fade there too. The step is now host code that can run on any copy of a particle's record, with the bounce as host code. While the game walks its emitters, the particles that step would move are collected into a batch instead; at the end of the particle manager a worker thread on another core steps the batch and computes the draws' values. The game thread waits for it only before anything reads a particle again (in practice at the frame's end, and it never had to wait). Emitters that can hurt a colossus (a damage test per particle) are still stepped on the game thread, in order, so the random numbers the step uses come out in the same sequence.
rows.result: Exact: an in-run check steps every deferred particle again on the game thread and compares it byte for byte: 2.13 million particles on the attract demo and 1.79 million at the lake, 0 differences; the draw values 3.36 million, 0 differ. Pictures: the gallop dust unchanged; the lake route shows the shrine view (the camera stays there), so the water was not on screen. Speed (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B, two seeds): frame time -0.10 / -0.11 ms on the attract demo and -0.10 / -0.09 ms at the lake, a small gain: the lake runs alone fall short of z 2 per seed (1.7, 1.8); kept because all four agree (pooled z about 4) and the check is exact. A job is about 95 particles, 0.08 ms on the worker. SOTC_S5PTCL on.

rows.summary: Round S6, the second collision round after S2. First the measuring routes: the 'lake' route used since S2 went back to the shrine at frame 7 600 (its second teleport is the console card's own place on the altar), so most 'lake' A/Bs measured the altar, and the r141 'ride' route never mounted Agro. New routes: lake6 (Avion's lake, Wander swimming, no return) and ride6 (the plain on the attract demo's path: Wander calls Agro and runs in wide turns, and mounts when he reaches Agro's side, not at a fixed frame). The profile at the lake put the two water probes on top of the collision queries: each probe walked the whole water mesh (S2's box and height tests on ~75 triangles a call, ~22 calls a frame). S6 gives each water mesh a host index (an xz grid of candidate triangles and the heights sorted with a range maximum), made and checked against guest memory every frame by a worker thread; a probe now visits the ~1.5 triangles S2's loop would actually test, in the same order. The game thread uses an index only in the frame after the worker vouched for it.

rows.summary: Round V2, after the console report that the game stopped loading or stopped moving after leaving it by accident (the PS button to LiveArea, or sleep) and coming back. The Vita suspends the whole process and invalidates its ux0: file handles on the way back: the disc image handles the port caches for good failed every read from then on (every load hung), the memory card image (kept open all session) could not be written, and the logs stopped. The display pacing also read a vcount jump of 9+ minutes (or a counter reset) as a step back and could hold the picture, the render thread and the game for up to 9 minutes. V2 reopens a disc file by its path when a read fails (retried for up to 10 s), reopens the card image and the logs after a resume, makes the vcount never go back and bounds a picture's slot to 0.5 s, and adds a watcher thread (ScePower's resume callback, or a 3 s wall-clock gap) that sets the CPU / GPU clocks again after a resume. A test knob (SOTC_TEST_SUSPEND) simulates a suspend in Vita3K: game thread stopped, disc reads and audio held, handles closed behind their caches, vcount set back.
rows.result: In Vita3K every read on a closed handle failed (0x80010051) and went through after the reopen; loads under way during a 3 s, 5 s, 8 s or 60 s simulated suspend finished, the card write path worked (also through a failed write), the sound went on and the game kept going (walk route to 9 138 frames, Wander walking before and after). A first version also moved the EE scheduler's VBlank deadlines on a resume and stuck the walk route's load for good; it was taken out (the scheduler already caps a gap at 8 VBlanks). Normal path unchanged apart from a relaxed load per picture; 0 sp-based NEON accesses. To confirm on the console: PS button mid-gallop and mid-load, sleep 1 min and 10+ min, then a save.

rows.summary: Round S8, the characters on the ride. First the map of S7's 6 ms of character work riding (Vita3K): it is a chain inside each character's frame (root dynamics and fitting with collision, node interpolation, IK and gaze, the pose, the layout, the cloths, the anime tables), flat (no symbol above 1%), and its results are read within 0.04-0.4 ms (the camera reads Wander, Wander's scripts read Agro). SOTC_S8CLOTH ships off; riding, no 2 ms of character work can run beside the game thread as the code is, and the levers left are the chain's own costs (motion keys, IK helpers, ~0.1-0.3 ms each) and the display's per-object chain.

rows.summary: Round S9, the game thread's Runtime bucket on the ride (Vita3K: 11% of the game thread, 3.5 ms a frame), broken down by caller from the sampler's LR and a measuring build that counts library calls by caller. The largest real item was the renderer's cache eviction: riding the heap sits over its high mark, so every ~16 frames a heap-only pressure pass walked ~7 600 meshes and every draw's ids into hash sets and evicted nothing; S9 runs that pass over the in-heap textures alone (the same evictions). It also drops S5's per-frame clock stamp and the display hooks' frame-log clock reads (~275 syscalls a frame with the console's frame log), copies the camera parameters without newlib's long-copy call, reads the skinned shadow palette straight into its job and stops zeroing 512 bytes of VU0 registers per ctrlTurn call. The dispatch, scheduler and syscall layers were priced (~0.6 ms together) but not removed.
rows.result: Exact: the in-run check compared 846 eviction passes, 50 928 shadow palettes and 17 378 camera copies over a whole ride, 0 differences. Interleaved A/B (Vita3K 222 MHz, off - on): ride7 +0.44 ± 0.35 ms (seed 7) and +0.38 ± 0.19 ms (seed 11), lake and attract no change; on by default. The ~1.9 ms the brief hoped for is not in this bucket: the SceLibKernel imports' 2.6% is mostly Vita3K charging a per-frame wait to whichever import call sits there (removing one moves the samples to the next), veneers are 0.29 ms (a link-order fix, not A/B-able), and the guest dispatch, scheduler checkpoints and isys syscalls are ~0.6 ms that stay until the remaining EE threads and recompiled callees become host code.

rows.summary: Round S13 carried on S11's list: the motion root's packed (int16) keys, which S11 had left to the recompiled function because ~0.2% came out one or two units apart, the next motion getters on S11's named views, and the EE scheduler's time slice. The packed-key mismatch turned out to be the emulator, not the arithmetic: the same host routine run again after the recompiled leg gave the leg's bits; the first answer had its products rounded to nearest although the FPSCR read toward zero. The trigger is the FPU divide of a zero (a motion at a whole frame), which switched the rounding mode with two FPSCR writes; Vita3K's recompiler then kept rounding to nearest for a while. S13 answers 0 / x and sqrt(0) as the signed zero they are in every mode (no switch), computes the packed keys on the host, makes GetMotionRootIntFrame and GetMotionRootInfo host routines, routes every caller of the root key through the views, keeps two option-node getters' recompiled functions in pointers, stretches the time slice while nothing could preempt, and fixes the camera round's root key (ctl126) to read the constant / packed data where the original does.
rows.result: Exact: the in-run check (a kernel call before each compared call so both legs see the FPSCR's mode) compared 1 056 633 calls riding (ride7), 609 759 at the lake (lake6) and 656 901 in the attract demo: 0 differences in outputs, v0, f0, the FPU condition bit and the VU0 registers. Interleaved A/B (Vita3K 222 MHz, off - on): ride7 +0.12 ± 0.19 ms (seed 7, 800 s) and -0.10 ± 0.23 ms (seed 11, 400 s): even, so off by default (SOTC_S13MOT=1 turns it on; the console's A/B can try it). The pieces replaced were only ~0.1 ms a frame; the scheduler's slow checkpoints riding are event unwinds, not the slice (~1 a frame saved). Left: the motion-curve evaluators (0.18%, ~1 500 MIPS instructions), GetMotionRootInfo's looping path, GetMotionRootDirInfo.

The hook and the skinned shadow read each skinned bone palette back out of the instance chain's second packet (readChainPaletteLean 0.42-0.57% of the game thread riding: the VIF codes walked twice, every qword copied with a bounds check, read note and prefetch); the lights are a 128-byte copy (left). Wander climbed Malus' hand, rode Cenobia's armoured back and climbed in Celosia's arena, and the aid's stabs fired 21+ times on Malus, but the hit never reached the colossus' damage record, so no point broke and no colossus died this round. 38 functions converted (D16's 36 still unchecked plus 2 new from these routes), 4 reached and checked exact (Cenobia's script command, the player's final blow, a torch release, a camera rewind), none slower: 4 ship behind SOTC_LIFTD18 (on).

rows.summary: Round S17, the game thread's unwinds to the EE scheduler riding. Counted per episode (the game thread taken off by a checkpoint, up to its next dispatch): about one a frame, 90-94% of them the GS FINISH interrupt handler arriving while the game thread polls iosWaitGPFinish; the IOP's replies and the streaming / loader / sound threads they wake (4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11) run while the game thread waits for the render thread and almost never reach its checkpoints. But each old-path episode took 0.4-2.2 ms of host time and the pending flag was met by 72-131 checkpoints a frame: the game thread re-entered through the dispatcher in the middle of its sub-thread coroutines. SOTC_S17IOP (A/B s17iop) runs the scheduler's dispatch loop at the checkpoint itself, on top of the game thread's frames and in run()'s order (events, handlers, woken threads until they park, VU0 handed over), and lets the game thread's frames go on when it is picked again: pending checkpoints 0.2-0.6 a frame, slow checkpoints 15-18 instead of 85-146, an episode 46-76 us.
rows.result: Exact by its check: each episode the old way or nested at random, both paths' kernel calls in order hashed: 11 451 episodes riding (99.6% in orders both paths produce, the common ones in the same proportions), 8 997 at the lake (99.4%), 10 204 in the attract demo (99.7%); no bail-out, no unparked wake. Interleaved A/B (Vita3K 222 MHz, off - on): ride7 +0.156 ± 0.168 ms (seed 7, 800 s) and -0.005 ± 0.250 ms (seed 11, 800 s), lake6 -0.142 ± 0.191, attract -0.008 ± 0.313; a 150-frame block A/B +0.41 ± 1.06 (scenery-dominated). Not z > 2: off by default (SOTC_S17IOP=1); the per-frame A/B may hide the old path's expensive state (it needs several old episodes in a row), so the console's A/B decides. Boots and rides with 89 MB taken; pictures normal; no sp-based NEON accesses.

rows.summary: Round S16 took S14's next display item: the model draw plans (each model's packets of one LOD, kept across frames since round 8) were checked against the guest packet list every frame they were used (two cache lines of PS2-shaped model data, the whole list hashed one frame in 16), 0.17% of the game thread riding (~0.05 ms). S16 hooks the game's own model setup calls instead: modelInitialize (the setup of a model file just read from the disc), modelReInitialize (its setup again after the heap's garbage pass moved and relocated it) and modelInitDispModelClass. Each call withdraws the stamps of that model's plans; a stamped plan is used with no guest read, a withdrawn one is checked in full once. The first builds also withdrew every stamp at each garbage move, but riding the garbage pass keeps moving blocks and the full re-checks cost as much as they saved; the shipped build trusts modelReInitialize for moved models and uses 99.8% of the plans unchecked riding.
rows.result: Exact: with the check on, every plan used unchecked was also checked the old way: 522 046 riding (mounted), 168 548 at the lake and 168 664 in the attract demo, through 17 460 garbage moves and 10 021 setup calls, 0 differences. Speed even, as expected for ~0.05 ms (Vita3K 222 MHz, interleaved A/B, off - on): ride7 -0.09 +- 0.37 / +0.06 +- 0.25 ms (seeds 7 / 11), lake6 +0.11 +- 0.26, attract -0.03 +- 0.25: off by default (SOTC_S16PLAN=1 turns it on; the console's A/B can judge it).
